title: Cabinet approves $ 200 m ADB financing for MSME financial sector development | Daily FT

Wednesday, 11 November 2026 00:30

The Cabinet of Ministers has approved entering into financing agreements with the Asian Development Bank (ADB) to secure $ 200 million for a sector development program aimed at strengthening access to finance for micro, small and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs).

The financing comprises a $ 100 million policy-based loan from the ADB’s ordinary capital resources and a further $ 100 million through a financial intermediation loan component.

Addressing the weekly post-Caninet meeting media briefing yesterday, Cabinet Spokesman and Minister Dr. Nalinda Jayatissa said the approval follows the Cabinet decision of 16 March 2026 to conduct loan negotiations with the ADB for a broader $ 620 million policy-based financing package structured under five sub-programs. The package is intended to support Sri Lanka’s reform agenda alongside the International Monetary Fund’s (IMF) program.

He noted that discussions were held to secure the $ 200 million loan under two distinct repayment frameworks. “The $ 100 million policy-based component carries a 12-year repayment period with a three-year grace period. The remaining $ 100 million financial intermediation component has a 15-year repayment period alongside a five-year grace,” he added.

Following that approval, Dr. Jayatissa said the Department of External Resources has concluded formal financing discussions with the ADB on the first sub program, titled the ‘Sector Development Program for Developing a Strong and All-Inclusive Financial Ecosystem for Micro, Small and Medium-sized Enterprises’.

He said the latest Cabinet approval authorises the Government to enter into the relevant financing agreements with the ADB to implement the program.

The proposal to this effect was submitted by President Anura Kumara Dissanayake in his capacity as the Finance, Planning and Development Minister.

title: ADB approves $ 98 m loan to advance digital transformation in Sri Lanka | Daily FT

The Asian Development Bank (ADB) yesterday said it has approved a $98 million loan to support Sri Lanka’s efforts to build an inclusive, secure, and resilient digital economy, enhance public service delivery, and strengthen the foundations for private sector-led growth.

The Advancing Digital Transformation Project will help expand high-quality broadband connectivity and improve government data infrastructure, while reinforcing institutional capacity for cybersecurity and data protection and enhancing digital skills across the public sector.

The project aims to boost digital inclusion and equity by expanding access to digital government services for citizens and businesses, particularly women and underserved communities. 

ADB is providing an additional $1 million technical assistance grant from its Technical Assistance Special Fund to support program preparation, design, and capacity building for the executing and implementing agencies.  

“Sri Lanka has made strong progress in stabilising its economy and is now prioritising digital transformation as a key driver of inclusive growth and productivity,” said ADB Country Director for Sri Lanka Shannon Cowlin. “This project will help bridge connectivity gaps, improve the reliability and security of digital systems, and strengthen institutions to deliver better services to citizens and businesses.”

According to the ADB, despite high mobile coverage, access to reliable, high-speed broadband remains uneven, particularly in rural and underserved areas. Gaps in digital and data infrastructure, cybersecurity, data protection, and skills continue to constrain the delivery of efficient public services and limit private sector development. 

The project will address these challenges through a comprehensive, whole-of-Government approach aligned with the Government’s National Digital Economy Blueprint, the multilateral bank said.

The project will expand high-quality broadband connectivity in underserved areas; upgrade telecommunications infrastructure and boost services from 2G to 4G and 5G; and make Government data systems more reliable, interoperable, and resilient through an enhanced Lanka Government Cloud 3.0. It will bolster cybersecurity protection, including monitoring and incident response for government agencies deemed as critical national information infrastructure. It will also improve digital skills to build institutional capacity by training public sector employees, with targeted support to increase women’s participation in the digital economy.

By strengthening digital infrastructure and institutions, the project is expected to improve access to essential services such as health, education, and administrative services, reduce transaction costs, and expand economic opportunities. It will also enhance resilience by supporting secure, continuous digital systems that are critical to emergency response and service delivery.

Diversified conglomerate CIC Holdings PLC yesterday said it reported a consolidated revenue of Rs. 42.91 billion for the first half of the financial year 2026/27 (1H27). The Group maintained steady top-line growth of 3.06% and achieved a strong bottom-line expansion, with Profit After Tax (PAT) increasing by 16.72% to Rs. 3.79 billion. This is compared to Rs. 3.25 billion in the corresponding period of the previous year, notwithstanding Agri cluster movements shifting from the second quarter to the third quarter of the financial year.

The Group’s performance was supported by strong operational execution, margin expansion, and enhanced earnings contributions from equity-accounted investees. 

Operating profit (EBIT) strengthened to Rs. 5.86 billion, recording a 2.65% YoY growth, while profit before tax (PBT) rose to Rs. 5.35 billion (up 8.26% YoY). During the period under review, Agri Solutions remained the Group’s largest revenue contributor, accounting for approximately 40.18% of total gross segment revenue. Livestock Solutions and Health and Personal Care contributed around 24.29% and 23.08% respectively, while the Industrial Solutions segment accounted for 12.45% of total gross segment revenue.

Gross profit increased to Rs. 11.69 billion, representing a 4.36% year-on-year growth, supported by disciplined pricing and operational efficiencies. Gross profit margin improved to 27.25%, demonstrating strong profitability resilience. Importantly, this solid performance was recorded during the Group’s off-peak second quarter, despite the delayed rains pushing back the Agri season, underscoring CIC’s operational consistency and diversified earnings base.

During the period under review, key core operating sectors delivered strong results. Industrial Solutions delivered the strongest top-line expansion, with revenue surging 34.91% to Rs. 5.43 billion. Livestock Solutions recorded an 11.87% revenue growth to reach Rs. 10.59 billion, while Health and Personal Care revenue expanded by 6.40% to Rs. 10.05 billion. Agri Solutions contributed Rs. 17.51 billion to segment revenue.

In terms of profitability, Livestock Solutions recorded strong segmental profit growth of 30.86% to Rs. 1.52 billion, while Industrial Solutions expanded its segmental profit by 47.37% to Rs. 1.02 billion. The Health and Personal Care sector achieved a 10.02% increase in segmental profit to Rs. 1.43 billion, while Agri Solutions generated Rs. 1.63 billion in segment results. Overall, the Group’s core business sectors generated Rs. 5.60 billion in total segment results, representing a 3.85% year-on-year increase and reinforcing broad-based earnings resilience across key operating verticals.

The Group’s post-subdivision basic/diluted earnings per share (EPS) increased from Rs. 1.37 to Rs. 1.67, reflecting a 21.90% year-on-year improvement, supported by higher net profits attributable to equity holders. The balance sheet expanded significantly, with total assets surpassing the milestone to reach Rs. 108.58 billion (compared to Rs. 98.63 billion in H1FY26), while total group equity strengthened to Rs. 56.46 billion.

Group CEO Aroshan Seresinhe said: “This performance reflects the inherent resilience of our business model and the focused execution of our teams across key growth verticals. By strengthening our core operations in agriculture, healthcare, livestock, and industrial solutions, we have sustained strong profitability and margin discipline despite challenging economic conditions. Our commitment remains firm on nurturing vital supply chains, expanding our high-value product offerings, and supporting community livelihoods. As we move into the second half of the financial year, we will continue to focus on operational excellence, driving sustainable growth, and delivering long-term value to all stakeholders.”

title: Neil Marine Sports and Leisure launches Hidea outboard motors in Sri Lanka | Daily FT

Neil Marine Sports and Leisure Ltd., a member of the Neil Marine Group of companies has launched Hidea Outboard Motors in Sri Lanka, bringing a range of 2.5HP to 200HP two- stroke and four-stroke petrol, kerosene and electric engines to the local market under an exclusive agency agreement. 

The product was launched at the Granbell Hotel, Colombo, on 26 October, and the new product range targets fishermen, leisure boaters, commercial operators and marine professionals, offering a selection of engines designed to provide reliable performance, fuel efficiency and affordable operation. 

Addressing the gathering, Neil Marine Group CEO Shan Perera said the partnership marked a new chapter for the company, which has been building boats in Sri Lanka for more than five decades. 

“Since 1969, Neil Fernando and Company Ltd. has been building boats in Sri Lanka. Over more than five decades, we have delivered over 40,000 vessels to customers around the world. Everything we have achieved is based on three qualities - craftsmanship, trust and the dedication of our people,” he said. 

He noted that the partnership would enable the company to offer a complete marine solution to the customers by combining its boat-building expertise with Hidea’s engine technology. “A boat is only as good as the engine that drives it. For years, we have built the hull. Now, with Hidea, we can offer the power as well as a complete marine solution under one trusted brand name,” Perera said. 

He emphasised that the company’s objective was to introduce economical and dependable engines to the fisheries and tourism sectors, which are the two lifelines of the Sri Lankan economy. 

Highlighting the challenges faced by fishermen, he said fuel costs and engine breakdowns directly affected their family incomes and livelihoods. 

“For them, the boat is a livelihood. Every litre of fuel and every day lost to a breakdown comes straight out of the family income. They need an engine that is reliable, fuel-efficient and affordable to run and maintain. That is what we want to give them,” he said. 

Perera also identified marine tourism as a growing market for the new engines, particularly for whale watching, island transfers, fishing charters and leisure boating. 

He said tourism operators needed dependable and cost-effective engines to expand their services while ensuring safe and enjoyable experiences for visitors. 

The introduction of electric outboards was another important aspect of the partnership. Available alongside the petrol range under Hidea’s Ultimate Mobility vision, the electric engines offer quieter and cleaner propulsion options for environmentally sensitive marine locations.

“Quiet, clean and efficient, they are ideal for our lagoons, rivers and sensitive coastal waters, and for operators who want to give guests a calmer, more sustainable experience,” Perera said. 

He added that the partnership would bring benefits beyond individual boat owners and operators. “When fishermen earn more and tourism operators grow, the benefit reaches whole communities. That is the real value of tonight’s launch,” he said. 

Perera thanked the Hidea team for its confidence in Neil Marine Sports & Leisure and Sri Lanka, reaffirming the company’s commitment to quality products, reliable service and long- term customer support. 

Hidea China Regional Director Michael Zhou also spoke at the product launch and said the company had confidence in the Group. He added that the Hidea product range would contribute to boosting productivity in the fisheries industry and other sectors of the economy. 

Neil Marine Group Chairman Kumarie Fernando, Group President Manel Fernando, Managing Director Sail Lanka Indra Kaushal Rajapaksa, former Navy Commander Admiral Priyantha Perera, Fisheries Corporation Chairman Kapila Bamunuarachchi, industry partners, boat owners and members of the marine sector participated in the event. 

Founded in 1969, the Neil Marine Group is involved in boatbuilding, the manufacture of Styrofoam boxes and mattresses, and the import of brands such as Juki and Pegasus sewing machines and spare parts, Exclusive agent agreement marine engines Suzuki and HD Hyundai, Winner Kayak brand, VETUS Boat accessories, Fliexiteek and resins.

title: EFC launches publication on ‘Collective Bargaining and Agreements in Sri Lanka’ | Daily FT

The Employers’ Federation of Ceylon (EFC) has launched its latest publication ‘Collective Bargaining and Agreements in Sri Lanka’ (Volume 1) to provide a detailed overview of the collective agreements signed from 2022 to 2024 between EFC member companies and trade unions. 

The publication is the fruit of the research efforts by the EFC’s Research and Publications Unit. 

The EFC which is the national employers’ organisation and the constituent of the International Labour Organisation (ILO) in Sri Lanka, has consistently pursued its vision to promote industrial harmony through productive employment.  Through its proactive engagement with trade unions and Government bodies, the EFC has fostered a collaborative approach to industrial relations, promoting collective bargaining as means of conflict resolution which has ensured long-term industrial harmony. Now into its 97th year and representing a diverse set of industries with over 800,000 employees in Sri Lanka, the EFC has established itself as a significant pillar in industrial relations platforms in Sri Lanka. 

Collective bargaining process is a tool that can be used to create and enhance industrial relations between the employer and the employees. The foundation of the collective bargaining in Sri Lanka is a combination of statutory provisions, established practices/customs and mutual agreements. The mechanism provides a formal platform for discussion/ negotiations between employer and employee. 

Through such discussions and negotiations, the employees collectively or through trade unions will have the opportunity to table their concerns while the employers will have the opportunity to put forward their expectations. This will create a relationship that is more transparent and it will further reduce the communication gap between the employer and the employee. 

The first part of the monograph provides a brief snapshot of the legal framework and current practices which are applicable to the collective bargaining process in Sri Lanka, and the second part provides details of successfully signed collective agreements between 2022 and 2024.  

EFC Director General, Yashoravi Bakmiwewa said the substantial number of collective agreements signed between the selected period (2022-2024) represents the current trend of adopting the collective bargaining process as a forum of discussion between the employer and the employee. “The publication aims to serve as a valuable reference for employers, HR professionals, industrial relations practitioners, researchers and other stakeholders interested in understanding the developments in remuneration and employment benefits negotiated through the collective bargaining process,” Bakmiwewa added.

The data presented in the publication constitutes a consolidated representation of salary increments, benefits, and other compensation-related information collected from multiple organisations across key industries. The publication can be purchased at the EFC.

title: Ravi K appeals to HSBC to consider winding down HDPL in Sri Lanka | Daily FT
summary:

Opposition MP Ravi Karunanayake

Opposition MP Ravi Karunanayake has written personally to HSBC Holdings Group Chairman and Group Chief Executive appealing for the closure of HSBC Electronic Data Processing Lanka to be reversed, and offering to help assemble Government support for keeping the operation in the country.

The letter, addressed to both executives and titled a personal and national appeal, runs through the centre’s 22-year history, the bank’s stated reasons for the migration, and the livelihoods attached to 1,659 jobs. Karunanayake asks group leadership to reopen the decision and to talk before the move becomes irreversible.

He rests much of the appeal on the wording of the bank’s own notice. “Your notification of 7 October 2026 expressly states that the proposed migration follows a global operating-model review and does not reflect the performance of the Sri Lankan company. That acknowledgement provides a compelling reason to explore an alternative.”

He puts the workforce at 1,659 as at 30 September, 2026, and says the operation at its best employed about 4,500 young Sri Lankans. “Behind each position is a family, a set of responsibilities and a future built through years of dedication,” he wrote. Closure, he says, means “uncertainty and abandonment of their aspirations for generations children’s education, housing commitments, care for parents and the prospect of continuing a fulfilling professional life in their own country.”

Karunanayake, a former Minister of Trade and Commerce, Finance and Foreign Affairs, traces the investment to his first ministerial tenure between 2001 and 2004. He says he mooted bringing it to Sri Lanka and remains grateful to HSBC “for listening to my representations,  recognising our people’s potential, and translating that confidence into substantial investment and development of the Human Resources in Sri Lanka.”

The centre opened at the World Trade Centre in Colombo 1 in 2004. It later moved into a built-to-suit facility at 439 Sri Jayewardenepura Mawatha, Kotte, in his constituency, followed by Union Place, Colombo 2 in 2022 and Mireka Tower, Colombo 5. He says each was built to the bank’s Base Build Engineering Guidelines and Standards, and that the sites lifted both footprint and headcount.

“What began as an investment became a source of pride and possibility to ‘both’ our small nation and the HSBC brand a forerunner,” he wrote. “It demonstrated that our young people could meet global standards and contribute meaningfully.”

The letter concedes the commercial case rather than dismissing it. Karunanayake notes his later service as Finance and Foreign Affairs Minister and says he appreciates the bank’s responsibilities to shareholders, customers and employees. “Concerns about operating costs, workforce availability, scale and competitiveness merit a serious response. I believe we owe it to this longstanding partnership to examine together whether those concerns can be resolved.”

Though presently outside Government, he pledges to work with the administration and industry on retention. “I will do my utmost to work constructively with the Government, the relevant authorities and industry partners to facilitate every practicable measure that could sustain and renew HSBC’s operations here. I am prepared to advocate vigorously for the fullest support and benefits that can responsibly be made available, and to help address the obstacles to remaining competitive.”

He frames that offer as bipartisan. “Preserving opportunity for our people is a national responsibility that transcends political differences.”

The appeal is made principally on behalf of younger workers, who he says used the centre to acquire knowledge, work across cultures and build careers connected to the wider world. “The decision to exit from this operation would close an important avenue through which young Sri Lankans can realise their ambitions while remaining in their native country. Their aspirations deserve a central place in our deliberations.”

Karunanayake asks for specific negotiations. “I therefore respectfully request that HSBC’s Group leadership reopen this decision and allow an urgent, time-bound dialogue before the planned migration becomes irreversible. Let us identify the specific changes needed in costs, recruitment, training, infrastructure and policy, and work towards a credible proposition for retaining and reinvesting in the Sri Lankan operation.”

He sets the decision against the country’s recovery from its 2022 debt default. “Sri Lanka is striving to overcome profound difficulties, correct longstanding weaknesses and rebuild confidence in its future. This is precisely the moment when the support of established partners as HSBC is most needed.” A reversal, he argues, “would protect livelihoods and send a powerful message that recovery can be achieved through partnership, perseverance and shared endeavour.”

“I ask you, in that spirit, to look beyond the balance sheet of an individual operation and consider the wider national significance of this decision. The commercial questions must be answered, but so too must we recognise the value of the talent, loyalty and experience earned and nurtured here, and the hopes and aspirations that depend upon them.”

He closes on the original decision to invest. “When I initiated the birth of this project to Sri Lanka, I did so with faith in our people and in HSBC’s willingness to see their potential. That faith remains as strong today. Let us pool our talent, our resources and our determination to find a way forward.”

The Cabinet of Ministers has approved entering into an agreement with India to secure a financial grant for the purchase of 100 new ambulances for the 1990 Suwa Seriya emergency service.

Addressing the weekly post-Cabinet media briefing yesterday, Cabinet Spokesman and Health Minister Dr. Nalinda Jayatissa said the Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) will be signed during discussions with the Indian Health Minister, who is scheduled to arrive in Sri Lanka today (11).

He said the Government of India agreed to the grant following a special request from Sri Lanka. The ambulances will be fully equipped with medical facilities.

Responding to journalists’ questions on whether the financial assistance involves debt or restricted procurement, Dr. Jayatissa said the funds will arrive as an outright grant of Rs. 1,725.7 million.

He said the proposal will address wear and tear across the service’s emergency fleet. “As these ambulances cover around 9 million kilometers annually, the likelihood of mechanical faults occurring within the existing fleet of 322 ambulances has increased,” he said.

The 1990 Suwa Seriya free-of-charge service operates 24-hours, in all districts, handling between 1,000 and 1,200 patient transport requests daily. It was launched in 2016 with Indian financial assistance and expanded countrywide in 2018.

title: New railway bridge across Mahaweli river with Indian loan grant scheme | Daily FT

Cabinet Spokesman and Minister Dr. Nalinda Jayatissa

By Charumini de Silva 

The Cabinet of Ministers has approved constructing a new railway bridge across the Mahaweli River between Sarasavi Uyana and Peradeniya, with financial assistance from India.

The bridge will be constructed on the Matale railway line as part of efforts to improve railway connectivity and develop an extensive suburban railway network covering the Greater Kandy area.

Announcing the decision at the weekly post-Caninet meeting media briefing yesterday, Cabinet Spokesman and Minister Dr. Nalinda Jayatissa said funding for the project will be obtained through an Indian loan grant scheme intended for the renovation and development of railway infrastructure facilities damaged by Cyclone Ditwah.

He said the proposed bridge is expected to improve the integration of the Matale railway line with the national railway network.

“The Government is also planning to develop an extensive suburban railway network in the Greater Kandy area, with a feasibility study currently underway. The proposed development includes, converting the main railway line from Kadugannawa to Gampola via Peradeniya into a double-track railway line. Plans also include converting the Matale railway line between Peradeniya and Katugastota into a double-track railway line,” he added.

Dr. Jayatissa said the Government has also identified the need to address capacity constraints caused by the existing single-track railway infrastructure, while improving the reliability and connectivity of train services.

Responding to queries from journalists on whether construction of the new bridge would interrupt work on the historic Black Bridge (Kalu Paalama), he said the two projects would run side by side. 

“The restoration will carry on without interruption. Building the new bridge is happening alongside it,” he added.

The Cabinet Spokesman noted that the Black Bridge, a single-track structure first built in 1865, was badly damaged in the cyclone. Given its age and structural limitations, the Central Engineering Consultancy Bureau (CECB) is handling the repairs, with technical support from the University of Peradeniya.

The proposal to this effect was submitted by Transport, Highways and Urban Development Minister Bimal Rathnayake.

Bhanu Wijayaratne, a distinguished banking and financial services professional with over four decades of experience, was elected President-Elect of the Organisation of Professional Associations of Sri Lanka (OPA) for the 2026- 2027 term at the 51st Annual General Meeting, held on 30 October 2026. 

Following his tenure as President-Elect, he will assume the Presidency of the OPA for the 2027-2028 term. 

His election marks a significant milestone in a professional career in banking and finance, serving in senior executive leadership, institutional governance, professional service and a sustained commitment to the advancement of the country’s professional community.

An alumnus of the Royal College, Wijayaratne possesses an impressive portfolio of academic qualifications and professional credentials. He holds a Master’s Degree in Financial Economics from the University of Colombo and a Master of Business Administration (MBA) from the University of Manipal. He is a Senior Fellow of the Institute of Bankers of Sri Lanka (FIBs -SL) and a Fellow of the Institute of Chartered Professional Managers (FCPM). He also holds   membership of the Institute of Internal Auditors, USA (Sri Lankan Chapter). Beyond his distinguished career in banking and financial services, Wijayaratne possesses a strong grounding in economics and maintains professional memberships in both the Sri Lanka Economic Association and Institute of Quality and Productivity Management- Sri Lanka.  

Over the course of his distinguished career, he has undertaken several senior executive responsibilities in the banking and finance sector including Chief Compliance Officer, Chief Risk Officer, Chief Internal Auditor and Group Head of Audit. His areas of professional expertise encompass banking management, corporate governance, regulatory compliance, risk management and internal audit. These responsibilities have provided him with extensive exposure to institutional leadership, strategic decision-making and the governance frameworks essential to organisational integrity and effectiveness.

In conjunction with his corporate career, Wijayaratne has made a noteworthy contribution to professional education, knowledge and skills development. His academic engagements include lecturing at the College of Banking and Finance Studies of the Institute of Bankers of Sri Lanka and the Centre for Banking Studies of the Central Bank of Sri Lanka. He has also served as a visiting lecturer to graduate and postgraduate programs at several private universities and higher educational institutions, in addition to delivering lectures and professional development sessions at numerous institutions by invitation.

His commitment to professional service extends well beyond his corporate responsibilities. He has served the Association of Professional Bankers of Sri Lanka in several important leadership capacities, including Treasurer, Vice President and Senior Vice President, and currently serves on its Council of Advisors. He has also served as General Secretary and Chairman of the Association of Compliance Officers of Banks - Sri Lanka.

Within OPA, Wijayaratne has demonstrated sustained leadership and an active commitment to advancing the Organisation’s institutional mandate. Having served as Vice President and Chairman of the National Issues Committee (NIC) for three consecutive years, he has played an instrumental role in strengthening OPA’s engagement on matters of national importance and creating avenues through which multidisciplinary professional expertise to contribute towards public policy and national development.

Through the National Issues Committee, he has supported professional deliberations, seminars and initiatives addressing critical national concerns, including economic challenges, energy and supply-chain resilience, governance, anti-money laundering and countering   financing of terrorism (AML/CFT), public-sector effectiveness and environmental sustainability. His approach has consistently emphasised the importance of moving beyond discussion towards evidence-based recommendations, constructive engagement and practical outcomes.

He has also been actively involved in strengthening OPA’s engagement with Government institutions, exploring opportunities to mobilise the specialised knowledge and capabilities of its Member Associations in addressing national priorities. His vision recognises the considerable potential of OPA to serve as a credible professional resource to policymakers and public institutions.

In addition, Wijayaratne served as the Convener of the 39th OPA Annual Conference and Chairman of its Technical Sessions Committee, held under the theme “Envisioning Sri Lanka: Beyond Recovery.” The conference brought together distinguished personalities and professionals from diverse disciplines to deliberate on the challenges, opportunities and strategic imperatives shaping Sri Lanka’s future. 

His contributions to the Organisation have also extended to strengthening its external relations and broadening its international engagement. He played an instrumental role in initiating diplomatic engagement, including interactions with the Ambassador of Vietnam, which opened avenues for exploring areas of mutual interest in trade, investment and socioeconomic development. He has also contributed to the introduction of the OPA’s Anthem, an initiative that embodies the unity, shared identity and collective aspirations of Sri Lanka’s professional community

In presenting his vision for the Organisation ahead of his election as President-Elect, Wijayaratne advanced the theme, “Strengthening OPA: Uniting Professional Excellence for National Progress”, setting out a forward-looking agenda centred on institutional unity, the consolidation of professional excellence and a renewed commitment to national progress.

At the heart of this vision, lies the conviction that OPA’s greatest institutional strength is derived from the collective knowledge, professional expertise and intellectual capabilities of its 52 Member Associations from 32 diverse professions. He believes that the Organisation’s future influence will depend on its ability to unite these diverse professional constituencies and channel their collective strengths towards a common national purpose.-His proposed priorities encompass five key areas: strengthening unity and inclusiveness among Member Associations; translating professional expertise into tangible national impact; building strategic partnerships; enhancing OPA’s visibility and influence; and strengthening institutional effectiveness and continuity.

Wijayaratne’s vision seeks to build upon this institutional strength, fostering a more united, engaged and influential professional community while reinforcing OPA’s contribution to the economic, social and institutional progress of Sri Lanka.

His forthcoming leadership journey will therefore be guided by a clear and purposeful ambition: to strengthen the Organisation, unite its professional constituencies and translate the collective excellence of its membership into meaningful national progress, the OPA said.

title: Budget 2027 must turn fiscal discipline into long term growth path | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 11 November 2026 00:26
-     - 92

Introduction

On 12 November the President, Finance Minister, will present the 2027 Budget to a Parliament. The public that have grown used to fiscal good news have plethora of expectations. The numbers justify some of that optimism. In the first eight months of 2026, revenue and grants came in at Rs. 4,002 billion, an increase of 21% year-on-year and 75.5% of the annual estimate, when a pro-rata basis it would have been 66.7%. The Treasury ran an overall surplus of Rs. 35 billion for the period against a budgeted full-year deficit of Rs. 1,757 billion, and the primary surplus of Rs. 1,645 billion was almost double the Rs. 860 billion targeted for the whole year.

This remarkably different figures are not by accident. Under the IMF’s Extended Fund Facility, the fiscal target has been a primary surplus of 2.3% of GDP; the revised estimates for 2025 show 3.8%. Fiscal revenue, which collapsed to around 8% of GDP in 2021 after the 2019 tax cuts, is now close to 16%. Central government debt fell to 91.6% of GDP at end-2025 from 95.5% a year earlier. Few countries emerging from a sovereign default have consolidated this quickly. 

But a fiscal outturn has two sides, and the expenditure side deserves a closer look. Total spending to August was only 56.2% of the annual budget. Capital expenditure and net lending, at Rs. 436 billion, were just 31.8% of an allocation of roughly Rs. 1,369 billion. Execution of public investment in 2025 also fell short, at about 77% of the estimate. This is not part of fiscal discipline, in fact, under-execution of budgeted capital expenditure.

The distinction matters for growth. Restraint on recurrent spending improves the quality of fiscal adjustment. Curtailment on capital expenditure does the opposite: it lowers the economy’s future productive capacity, leaving fewer roads, irrigation schemes, transmission lines and hospitals, and a lower potential growth rate in subsequent years. It is the politically painless form of consolidation, because its cost shows up only years later in the form of slower growth. A surplus built on unspent capital expenditure is not something to celebrate for long.

Public debt: past the peak, not out of the woods

The debt ratio has turned, helped by primary surpluses, a recovery in nominal GDP and the restructuring of external debt. Yet it remains well above the 68–76% band held during 2006–2017, and interest still absorbs close to half of government revenue. The fiscal anchor cannot be loosened yet.

Limitations of the budget

Every year the run-up to the Budget Speech produces a long list of demands. Public servants want a salary revision, pensioners an allowance, professionals tax relief, importers lower duties, farmers fertiliser subsidies, and every electorate a new road or school building. There are very reasonable demands on its own, unfortunately, added together, they exceed any feasible fiscal envelope.

A national budget is not a magic wand. It is the principal instrument of fiscal policy, through which the government decides how much of national income it will absorb through taxation, how it will allocate that spending, and how it will finance the gap. Through these choices the government steers the economy in the direction it wishes to take. The question to ask on 12 November is not what the budget gives me or my group, but where it is taking the economy and whether the instruments chosen will get us there.

The Appropriation Bill tabled in Parliament provides for service expenditure of Rs. 4,993 billion, about 13% above the 2026 Bill, with a net borrowing limit of Rs. 3.8 trillion. Under the IMF program, the primary surplus must stay at 2.3% of GDP. The Budget Speech can reallocate within those limits. The IMF wants the government to present the budget within this agreed framework, continuing its commitment to the part of fiscal consolidation and debt sustainability.

Policy Consistency

Prior to the budget, indication of certain proposals of reasonable expectations  were in the public media.

The first is personal income tax relief. The personal relief, which is the tax-free threshold under the Advance Personal Income Tax (APIT), was raised from Rs. 1.2 million to Rs. 1.8 million a year, or Rs. 150,000 a month, from April 2025, while the 6% band was extended to Rs. 1 million. In September the Deputy Minister of Economic Development told Parliament that the government remains committed to raising the monthly threshold to Rs. 200,000, and the President has publicly promised tax relief in this budget. For the salaried middle class, it would be a welcome adjustment.

The trade-off should be stated plainly. When the threshold was last raised, the Finance Ministry estimated that around 200,000 of some 800,000 individual taxpayers would drop out of the net, at a cost of about Rs. 60 billion a year. A narrow direct tax base is precisely why we lean so heavily on regressive indirect taxes. 

The second is a rationalisation of indirect taxes. Taxes on goods and services are budgeted at Rs. 3,056 billion in 2026, against Rs. 1,210 billion from income tax, so the indirect tax structure effectively shapes our price level and our cost of production. That structure has become crowded, with VAT, the Social Security Contribution Levy (SSCL), Cess and other border levies layered on top of one another, several of them falling on intermediate and capital goods. Cascading levies of this kind raise the effective rate of protection for domestic sales and act as an implicit tax on exports. Removing them from inputs would support both investment and consumption, at a modest net revenue cost if VAT administration improves at the same time.

The third is policy consistency. Investors can price a high tax rate. What they cannot price is a tax code that changes with every budget. A medium-term revenue strategy, announced once and adhered to, would lower the risk premium on private investment more effectively than any single concession.

The fourth is a clear and well-communicated direction. Expectations drive investment decisions. The budget should set out where the government wants the economy to be in five years, explain the trade-offs involved, and then hold to that course.

The twin deficits: an old ailment

Behind the annual wish lists lies the structural problem that has taken Sri Lanka to the IMF 17 times: the twin deficits. The government has persistently spent more than it collects as tax revenue, and the country has persistently spent more abroad than it earns. In national accounting terms, the current account deficit is simply the gap between domestic investment and domestic savings, and a large, persistent fiscal deficit is public dissaving. The two deficits therefore feed each other. Fiscal expansion raises domestic absorption, much of which leaks into imports, and the resulting external gap has been financed with foreign borrowing, a large share of it by the state itself.

Two features of our development model have kept this cycle going. The first is an excessive reliance on the government for certain activities that private capital could finance. Highways, power plants, ports and water schemes have been built almost entirely through the budget and state-owned enterprises, mostly on borrowed money. The 2026 Budget allocates 4.0% of GDP to public investment, while interest payments alone take 7.6%. A state whose interest bill is almost double its capital budget cannot remain the sole financier of national infrastructure.

Growth that does not earn its keep

The second feature is a growth model biased toward non-tradables. Non-tradable goods and services are those whose prices are determined in the domestic market because they cannot easily be traded across borders: construction, real estate, wholesale and retail trade, domestic transport, personal services and public administration. Tradables, by contrast, compete in world markets: manufactured exports, plantation crops, tourism, and IT and logistics services.

Growth driven by non-tradables looks impressive in the national accounts. But it generates income without generating foreign exchange, while the consumption it finances lifts import demand. Over time it also bids up domestic wages and prices relative to the rest of the world, appreciating the real exchange rate and squeezing the profitability of the export sector. External debt then rises faster than the economy’s capacity to service it. That, in essence, is the story of the decade that ended in default in 2022.

The ratio of exports to external debt reveals the story in a single line. In 2000, exports of goods and services were equal to about 69% of the country’s external debt. By 2020 the figure had fallen to 23%. It has since recovered to about 38%, but the improvement owes as much to debt restructuring as to export growth: total exports of goods and services were US$ 20.6 billion in 2025, up just 4.9%. Debt relief is a one-off. Only a larger export base can keep the ratio rising.

Two export engines losing momentum

Source’s Annual Reports 2000 and 2003; Sri Lanka Tea Board; EDB (2025); US$ billion

Our two traditional exports illustrate the problem. Apparel earnings rose from about $ 3 billion in 2000 to $ 5 billion in 2025, a compound growth rate of roughly 2% a year. In real terms, the industry earns no more today than it did a quarter of a century ago. Tea has done a little better in nominal terms, rising from $ 0.7 billion to $ 1.5 billion, but it has hovered around the same level for more than a decade as production volumes have stagnated. Together these two products still account for close to half of merchandise exports. An economy that has to service a debt stock of this size cannot depend on two mature industries growing at the pace of world prices. The need of export diversification has become yesterday’s problem rather than a future.

From consolidation to competitiveness

No single budget can unwind structural weaknesses built up over decades. What it can do is signal, clearly and credibly, a change of direction. Five areas deserve priority.

Crowd in private capital for infrastructure. Sri Lanka still lacks a comprehensive legal framework for public-private partnerships. The Cabinet approved the gazetting of a bill to establish a National Agency for PPPs only in October. The budget should commit to enacting it early in 2027, with competitive procurement, a transparent process for unsolicited proposals and full disclosure of the contingent liabilities the Treasury takes on, followed by a published pipeline of bankable projects in energy, transport, water and logistics. Well-structured PPPs allow the state to expand infrastructure without adding to its own balance sheet. Poorly structured ones simply move debt off budget. The law must guard against the latter.

Rebalance growth toward tradables. Incentives, tariff policy and public investment should be tilted toward activities that earn or save foreign exchange. That means a simpler, lower and predictable tariff schedule that does not tax imported inputs, faster VAT refunds for exporters, trade agreements that widen market access, and an end to the anti-export bias that makes selling at home more profitable than selling abroad. A competitive real exchange rate, sustained by fiscal discipline rather than administrative controls, is part of the same agenda.

Invest in human capital, beginning with the young. Unemployment among 20-24 year olds was 17.8% in 2025, close to five times the national rate of 3.9%, according to the Labour Force Survey. Only 49.4% of the population aged 15 and above participates in the labour force, and among women the figure is just 32.4%. Vocational training designed together with employers, English and digital skills, and the childcare and safe transport that allow women to take up paid work are not social spending. They raise both the economy’s labour input and its productivity in tradable sectors.

Allocate scarce resources more efficiently. For a small economy, Sri Lanka leaves a surprising share of its factor endowment idle:

nLabour: an ageing working-age population, half of it outside the labour force, while skilled workers continue to migrate.

nLand: large extents of state-owned land remain unused or underused. Long-term, bankable leases for agriculture, plantations, industry and energy would put it to productive use.

nRenewable energy: some of the best wind and solar resources in the region, particularly in the north and north-west. Harnessing them requires investment in the transmission grid and storage, and competitive, transparent procurement, so that lower-cost power reduces production costs across the export sector.

nStrategic location: Colombo lies beside the main east-west shipping lane, next to an Indian subcontinent whose cargo volumes continue to grow rapidly. Port capacity, transhipment, logistics and bunkering services built around that demand are tradables in the purest sense.

Protect capital spending in execution, not only in allocation. A larger capital vote that is only one-third spent by August achieves very little. Better project appraisal, multi-year expenditure commitments and quarterly public reporting on capital budget execution would do more for medium-term growth than a higher headline allocation.

The test

The stabilisation of the past three years is a platform, not a destination. Budget 2027 will be judged less by the relief it distributes than by the direction it sets. If it holds the fiscal anchor, ensures that public investment is actually delivered, opens infrastructure to private capital and tilts incentives toward what we can sell to the world, it will mark the point at which Sri Lanka moved from repairing its public finances to rebuilding its capacity to grow. If it does not, we risk repeating a familiar cycle: consolidation that looks good on paper, growth led by imports and non-tradables, and a debt problem that returns within a decade.

title: The money goes around: Does the Budget bring it back to the people? | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 11 November 2026 00:25
-     - 81

Imagine a small shopkeeper closing his shop after a busy day. A salaried employee notices deductions from a monthly salary. A mother pays taxes when she buys food, clothes and other household items. A business owner contributes while trying to keep a business alive and provide jobs. They may never read a national Budget or understand its complicated economic terms. But they share one simple expectation: the money they contribute should return to society in ways that make life better. They do not expect the Government to return the same money to their own pockets. They expect better schools for their children, reliable hospitals, safer roads, efficient public transport and more opportunities for the future.

A national Budget is a journey of public money from people to the Government, and back to society through services and development. The important question is not simply how much the Government collects or spends. It is whether people experience meaningful benefits in return.

From contributions to public services

The Government collects revenue from many sources, including income taxes, value added taxes, customs duties, fees and other levies. These resources are pooled to finance public services and national priorities. They support schools and hospitals, maintain roads, assist people in need and contribute to national development.

Public money is not an ordinary personal payment. The benefits are not expected to match each person’s contribution. A child from a low-income family may receive an education without paying school fees. An elderly person may depend on a public hospital. A village road may benefit hundreds of families who contribute different amounts to government revenue.

This is the purpose of public spending: to meet shared needs, widen opportunities and support people across society. The responsibility is to ensure that resources are allocated fairly and reach the people and communities who need them.

When spending does not become a difference

Consider a family that pays taxes but still struggles to obtain proper medical treatment. Parents may spend additional money on tuition because their children do not receive sufficient support at school. A small business owner may lose hours visiting several government offices to complete a simple task.


The Budget may have allocated money for hospitals, schools, roads and business development. But are people experiencing the improvements they expected?

A road may receive funding but remain unfinished. A hospital may acquire modern equipment without enough trained staff to operate it. A school may have a new building but lack teachers. An online service may be introduced, while people still need to visit several offices to complete an application.

In these situations, expenditure may be recorded, but the intended benefit remains out of reach. A school building matters when children learn better. Hospital equipment matters when patients receive timely treatment. A digital service matters when it saves people time and effort. The value of public spending is measured not only in money spent, but in lives changed.

This is why a Budget should be assessed beyond allocations and expenditure. It should be examined through the results people can see and experience.

Public money, public trust

People want to know that their contributions are being used responsibly. When they experience better services, fair treatment and careful management of public resources, confidence in public institutions can grow. They begin to see that their contribution has a purpose. The opposite happens when people encounter waste, delays, poor services or unfair treatment. Confidence fades, and they may begin to question whether the system deserves their trust.

This connection is particularly important in taxation. Tax collection is not only about laws, audits and penalties. People are more willing to meet their tax responsibilities when they believe the system is fair and public money is used for the country’s benefit.

The responsibility is shared, though not identical. Taxpayers are expected to comply with the law; the Government is responsible for managing public revenue wisely and delivering dependable services. A tax receipt records a contribution. The quality of public services helps people understand its wider value.

Learning from other countries

Some countries have explored ways to bring public spending closer to people’s needs.

New Zealand has applied a wellbeing approach to its Budget process since 2019. Its Treasury considers broader measures of wellbeing, including health, education, living conditions and quality of life. The message is clear: economic growth matters, but progress should also be reflected in how people live.

In Porto Alegre, Brazil, participatory budgeting gave residents opportunities to discuss community needs and influence local spending priorities. This experience showed how people could have a voice in deciding how public resources were used. It also demonstrated the importance of sustained institutional support for public participation.

South Korea offers a lesson in performance-based budgeting. Information on public programmes, including their relevance, efficiency and effectiveness, is used to inform budget decisions. This shifts attention beyond the amount allocated to what a programme is expected to achieve and whether it is delivering results.

These experiences differ, but they share a common principle: public spending should respond to people’s needs, and its results should be examined. Sri Lanka does not need to copy another country’s model. It can learn from these experiences and develop approaches suited to its own circumstances.

A practical pathway to accountability

A Budget promise should not disappear into a document, a meeting or a set of figures. It should lead to something people can see, use and feel in their daily lives.

Imagine a village waiting for a road, a mother hoping for better hospital care, or a child who needs a well-equipped classroom. They deserve to know what was promised, where the money went, what was delivered and whether life has improved.

Accountability begins when promises are clear, spending can be followed, results are honestly measured and people have a voice when something goes wrong. It is not about pointing fingers. It is about making sure public money does the job it was meant to do.

A promise made with public money must come with a result people can recognise.

Bringing the Budget closer to the people

For Sri Lanka, the challenge is not simply to allocate money, but to ensure that public spending leads to visible and meaningful improvements. This calls for clear priorities, responsible implementation, transparency and a willingness to examine whether programmes achieve their intended results. People should be able to understand what the Budget promises, how public money is used and what has been achieved. Communities should have opportunities to express their needs, while public institutions should explain their decisions and outcomes in language people can understand.

A Budget is not just a document prepared by the Government. It shapes the daily lives of people, in a child’s classroom, a patient’s hospital experience, a farmer’s access to roads, a business owner’s ability to complete a task and a family’s confidence in the future. The money goes around. But its journey is not complete when it reaches a public institution or when a project is recorded as expenditure. It is complete when the intended benefit reaches people.

Perhaps the most meaningful question we can ask about a national Budget is this: After all the money has been collected and spent, are people’s lives better?

That is the measure that matters. That is when the money truly comes back to the people.

The newly released preliminary results of the Household Income and Expenditure Survey (HIES) 2025 provide an important insight into this question. Despite substantial increases in nominal incomes, the typical Sri Lankan household had less purchasing power in early 2025 than it did nine years earlier, as reported in the 2016 HIES.

More strikingly, the decade has not affected households equally. While real incomes among the poorest households have fallen substantially, those at the upper end of the income distribution have recorded gains that hide the extent of the loss. The widening gap between average and median incomes further suggests that national averages increasingly conceal the experience of the typical household.

Nine years without an improvement in typical household income

According to the Department of Census and Statistics (DCS), average monthly household income increased from Rs. 62,237 in 2016 to Rs. 120,266 in early 2025, an increase of approximately 93%. However, much of this increase reflects inflation rather than improvements in purchasing power.

After adjusting for inflation, real mean household income increased by just 6% over the nine-year period. The experience of the typical household was worse. Real median monthly income fell from Rs. 43,511 in 2016 to Rs. 41,623 in 2025, a 4.3% decline. The comparison between 2016 and 2019 shows that real median household income increased by 7.6%. By early 2025, these gains had disappeared, with real median income falling 11.1% below its 2019 level.

A lost decade, but not for everyone

The national figures conceal an even more important development: household incomes have followed sharply different trajectories across the income distribution.

After adjusting for inflation, average monthly income among the poorest 20% of households declined from approximately Rs. 14,843 in 2016 to Rs. 12,403 in early 2025, a reduction of 16.4%. In contrast, average real income among the richest 20% increased from approximately Rs. 158,072 to Rs. 184,129, a gain of 16.5%. The divergence is pronounced after 2019, as the COVID-19 pandemic, the economic crisis, and other external shocks produced a decline in real income among the poorest quintile by approximately 19.6%, while income among the richest quintile increased by approximately 6.8% between 2019 and 2025. 

The average income ratio between the richest and poorest quintiles rose from 10.6 in 2016 to 11.2 in 2019 and 14.8 in early 2025. In other words, the households in the richest quintile earned, on average, nearly 15 times as much as those in the poorest quintile in 2025, compared with approximately 11 times in 2016. These suggest the limited improvement in national average income has concentrated at the top end of the distribution while accompanied by a much weaker experience among households at the lower end of the distribution.

The growing distance between the average and typical household

Another revealing finding is the widening difference between mean and median household income. In 2016, average household income was approximately 43% higher than median income. This relationship remained almost unchanged in 2019. However, by early 2025, average income was nearly 59% higher than median income. The divergence reflects their different trajectories; between 2019 and 2025, real mean household income declined by only 1.7%, while real median income fell by 11.1%.

This suggests the mean is influenced by high incomes, while the median represents the household at the midpoint of the income distribution. As a result, improvements among higher-income households can sustain the national average even when the typical household experiences declining purchasing power. Taken together, the widening mean–median gap and growing richest-to-poorest quintile income ratio point towards an increasingly uneven income distribution. However, these indicators are not substitutes for a comprehensive measure of inequality. The 2019 HIES reported an income Gini coefficient of 0.46, compared with 0.45 in 2016. The forthcoming full HIES 2025 results will be important for establishing whether this broader measure has also changed.

Poverty: The hidden U-curve

The latest poverty estimates reinforce concerns about the reversal of earlier progress. Sri Lanka’s poverty headcount declined from 16% in 2016 to 14.3% in 2019. However, the preliminary HIES 2025 findings estimate that poverty returned to 16%. The lack of household data between 2019 and 2025 likely hides a peak in poverty that occurred during that period, as the country experienced a plethora of shocks. The World Bank’s revised estimates suggest poverty may have peaked at around 20% during this period.

Recovering the economy must mean recovering household incomes

Sri Lanka’s return to economic growth is an important achievement. However, the latest HIES results demonstrate why national economic recovery cannot be assessed solely through aggregate indicators. Nearly a decade after 2016, the typical household has lost purchasing power, poverty reduction has returned to its earlier starting point, and income trajectories have diverged substantially between poorer and richer households.

The key question is no longer simply whether Sri Lanka’s economy is recovering, but whether that recovery is reaching households across the income distribution. A sustainable recovery therefore requires more than restoring economic output to transform it into something durable. It must translate into sustained growth in real household earnings, more productive employment opportunities, and greater resilience among economically vulnerable households.

(The author is a research fellow at the Institute of Policy Studies of Sri Lanka)

title: Taxed at the till: why the Government must keep its word | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 11 November 2026 00:23
-     - 78

Tomorrow, President Anura Kumara Dissanayake, who is also the Minister of Finance, will present the 2027 Budget to Parliament. He will have impressive revenue figures to report. Tax revenue rose from Rs. 1.75 trillion in 2022 to Rs. 5.05 trillion in 2025, and collections grew by a further 25.9% in the first half of this year.

Stability deserves recognition, and no responsible person wants to return to the queues of 2022. Yet the Budget must answer a harder question, which is, who has paid for this recovery? In 2025, 77.4% of tax revenue came from indirect taxes and only 22.6% from income tax. For every rupee collected directly, about Rs. 3.40 was collected at the till, at the pump and at the port. In the first half of this year, the balance tilted further, to 79% indirect and 21% direct.

An indirect tax takes no account of means. A teacher, a three-wheeler driver and a company chairman pay the same VAT on the same item, but it takes a far larger share of the teacher’s income and the driver’s. Dr W. A. Wijewardena, a former Deputy Governor of the Central Bank, recently described the country’s tax burden as an “overdose”. That is the right word for what many households are now experiencing.

What it costs a family of four

The Department of Census and Statistics has put the official poverty line at Rs. 17,592 per person per month in June 2026. That is about Rs. 586 a day. For a family of four, it comes to Rs. 70,368 a month, simply to meet basic needs.

This is a floor, not a comfortable standard of living. It is also one on which tax continues to bite. Suppose a family spends Rs. 30,000 of that monthly sum on goods and services carrying VAT at 18%. Some Rs. 4,576 of that spending is VAT alone, which is nearly two days of the family’s entire minimum budget. That is before we count the duties, excise and levies built into the prices it pays. Essential foods may be exempt, but fuel and cooking gas lost their exemptions in 2024, and every family feels those costs in its transport, its kitchen and its shopping bill.

What households actually spend tells the same story. According to preliminary findings of the Department of Census and Statistics’ Household Income and Expenditure Survey (HIES) 2025, average monthly household expenditure reached Rs. 116,191 in early 2025, an increase of 84.1% on the Rs. 63,130 recorded in 2019. Median spending nearly doubled, from Rs. 47,544 to Rs. 94,057.

Yet, measured at 2016 prices, the picture is very different. Real average monthly spending rose only from Rs. 55,430 to Rs. 63,734, an increase of about 15%, and real median spending from Rs. 41,745 to Rs. 51,593. In plain terms, households are paying far more but consuming only modestly more. Most of the increase has gone on higher prices, not better living standards, and the taxes built into those prices are part of the reason.

The burden is not evenly spread. Urban households spend an average of Rs. 158,023 a month, about 36% above the national average; rural households spend Rs. 108,918, and estate households only Rs. 88,691. A tax levied on consumption takes no account of these differences. The same survey shows how thin the margins have become. Average household income was Rs. 120,266 a month, leaving the typical household only about Rs. 4,000 after its spending. Estate households, with an average income of Rs. 72,558, spent more than they earned. For these families, every rupee of tax on necessities bites hardest.

The HIES also gives the Government the evidence it needs to act. The survey divides household spending into 35 categories, 19 for food and 16 for other goods and services. It shows exactly where ordinary families spend their money, and therefore where relief from VAT and other indirect taxes would do the most good.

A pledge is a debt

In August 2024, at Tangalle, then presidential candidate, Dissanayake, said that an NPP Government would remove VAT on medicines, medical tests, school items and supplementary reading books, and that it would do so from its first budget. Voters were entitled to take him at his word.

Two budgets later, parents are still waiting on school books. In September, the President told a rally at Nochchiyagama that plans were being prepared to remove the tax. Last month, he spoke of reducing VAT rates over the next two to three years. These are welcome words, but a child cannot read a statement of intent, and a parent cannot pay for books with one. The 2027 Budget should remove this tax outright and from a fixed date.

Hospital equipment and IT services belong on the same list. Medical machinery and equipment lost their VAT exemption when the rate rose to 18% in January 2024, and the cost of taxing the tools of treatment falls, sooner or later, on the patient. Local IT services have also carried 18% VAT since that date, when an exemption introduced to support the sector was withdrawn. This was the previous administration’s decision, but it is now this Government’s to correct. A country that wants its schools, small firms and public services to go digital should not make the means of doing so more expensive.

From a motorbike to a small car

During the election campaign, people were encouraged to believe that a motorbike, and then a small car, would come within reach of ordinary families. For a young worker, a small trader or a parent on the school run, this was never a matter of status. Where public transport remains inadequate, a vehicle is how people get to work and earn a living.

The reality is sobering. By mid-October last year, according to Sri Lanka Customs, 142,524 imported motorcycles had yielded Rs. 30.37 billion in taxes, an average of more than Rs. 210,000 on each machine. For cars, analysts have put the cumulative tax burden at between about 120% and more than 300% of the import value, because VAT and the Social Security Contribution Levy are charged not only on the vehicle but also on the duties already levied on it. One analyst had estimated that the vehicle sector had supplied some Rs. 905 billion, or almost 18%, of last year’s tax revenue. A 50% surcharge on customs import duty for cars and other vehicles was added in May and has since been extended to the end of the year. The Government may argue that this protects the rupee. It should also explain to a family saving for a first motorbike when, if ever, that promise will be met.

Prudence brings money home

Good tax policy looks beyond the next collection target. Sri Lanka needs foreign exchange, investment and enterprise, and those who can provide them have choices. The professional earning abroad, the exporter and the investor each decide where their money will sit. If rates climb and rules keep shifting, the rational decision is to keep it outside.

Consider the recent signals. Income from the export of services now bears a 15% income tax. Withholding tax on interest has doubled to 10%. VAT on financial services was raised to 20.5% in July, absorbing the separate 2.5% levy. Each measure can be defended on its own, but together they tell those with money to bring home that the next increase may be only a gazette away.

The Government should send the opposite message that moderate rates, a tax schedule held stable for several years, simple rules and a clear reward for foreign earnings brought into Sri Lanka through our banks. Every dollar that comes home and is invested here supports the rupee without a surcharge, creates work and, in time, widens the tax base far more durably than another levy on consumption.

Simpler taxes, better aimed: lessons from the region

Relief on particular items is necessary, but it is not enough. Our tax system must also become simpler and better targeted. An imported car, for example, carries customs duty, a surcharge on that duty, excise duty, a luxury tax, VAT and the 2.5% Social Security Contribution Levy, and the last two are charged on the other taxes as well as on the car itself. The levy’s exemption for imported motor vehicles was withdrawn in May. Other imports carry their own mix of duties, cesses and port levies. Few citizens, and not many businesses, can say with confidence what tax they are paying, or why. Complexity of this kind is costly twice over as it burdens the honest trader with paperwork, and it offers the dishonest one places to hide. And a system that charges the same standard rate on a child’s school book as on a consumer luxury is not targeted at all.

Our nearest neighbour shows that it can be done. For eight years, India has levied its Goods and Services Tax (GST) at four main rates of 5, 12, 18 and 28%, with a compensation cess on top of the highest band. On 22 September 2025, following a unanimous decision of the GST Council, it collapsed these into two principal rates - 5% for essentials and 18% as the standard rate. A separate 40% rate is reserved for tobacco, aerated drinks, large cars and other sin and luxury goods. Fewer rates mean fewer arguments over which rate applies, and less room for disputes and evasion.

Simplification went hand in hand with targeting. It is instructive to see what India did with the very items our own Government promised to relieve.

In a single reform, India took the tax off the school bag and the medicine cabinet, brought the family motorbike closer within reach, and asked those buying luxury vehicles to pay more. That is very close to what Sri Lankan voters were promised at Tangalle. Nor did India’s revenue collapse, although there was a cost. Gross GST collections grew by only 0.7% in November 2025, the first month to reflect a full month of the lower rates, and analysts have noted that higher spending had not, at first, made up for the cuts. Collections had then recovered, rising by 6.1% year on year in December, and reached a record ₹2.43 lakh crore in April 2026, although much of that growth came from tax on imports. Revenue held up even as rates came down.

India has applied the same thinking to direct taxes. Since its 2025 Budget, an individual under the new regime pays no income tax on income of up to ₹12 lakh (₹1.2 million) a year, and the rates above that rise in clear steps of five percentage points to a top rate of 30%. On 1 April 2026, the Income-tax Act, 2025 has replaced a law that had stood since 1961. The new Act has changed no rates; its purpose is to be understood. It roughly halves the length of the law, from about 512,000 words to 260,000, reduces the number of sections from 819 to 536, and replaces the confusing distinction between the “previous year” and the “assessment year” with a single “tax year”. Citizens should be able to read the law under which they are taxed.

Others in the region have chosen targeting over blanket increases. When Indonesia’s VAT was due to rise from 11 to 12% on 1 January 2025, President Prabowo Subianto confined the increase to luxury goods and services already subject to the luxury sales tax, such as private jets, yachts and luxury homes, and left ordinary goods at the old rate. Vietnam cut its standard VAT rate from 10 to 8% in 2022 and has extended the cut several times, currently to 31 December 2026, while excluding sectors such as banking, finance, telecommunications and real estate. Neither country abandoned fiscal discipline. Each simply decided, with care, who should carry the load.


The lesson for Sri Lanka is not to copy any one country, but to follow the same principles that a small number of clear VAT rates; a nil or low rate on books, medicines, medical equipment and other necessities; higher rates reserved for genuine luxuries, with relief aimed, using the HIES data, at what ordinary households actually buy; a single, transparent tax on vehicles in place of today’s stack of duties, levies and surcharges; and a tax law written so that an ordinary taxpayer can understand it. The Government has itself said that it plans to simplify the tax system from next year, and the 2027 Budget is the place to show how. It has also shown that consolidation is possible and that from July, VAT and the Social Security Contribution Levy on financial services were merged into a single rate of 20.5%. The same logic of one tax, one rate and one return should now be applied across the board and used to lower the burden rather than to raise it.

There is room to act

It will be said that there is no fiscal space and that our commitments to the International Monetary Fund (IMF) must be respected. They must. But as Dr Wijewardena has pointed out, revenue has already exceeded the program’s target of 15% of GDP. The IMF’s own figures show that last year’s primary surplus reached 5.4% of GDP, more than double the program’s target of 2.3%. Dr Wijewardena has also noted that only 28% of this year’s capital budget had been spent by the end of September. A Government collecting more than its program demands, while failing to spend what Parliament has already approved, can find room for relief on books and hospital equipment. Better compliance and a wider direct tax base can make up the difference over time.

The President has the mandate and the opportunity. On 12 November, he should remove VAT from school books, hospital equipment, medical services and IT services; commit to fewer, simpler tax rates, aimed at those most able to pay; set out a dated path to lower VAT and to a fair vehicle tax; and give those holding money abroad a stable reason to bring it home. Recovery will be real when a family of four can feel it, and not only when the Treasury can count it.

(The author is a President’s Counsel and a Member of Parliament)

title: Colombo under water: Is drainage system ready for challenges of a changing climate? | Daily FT
summary:
