-     - 58

Colombo National Hospital

The floods that inundated several parts of Colombo on November 06, 2026 have once again exposed the vulnerability of Sri Lanka’s commercial capital to heavy rainfall. This incident highlights the urgent need for a comprehensive assessment of the capacity and adequacy of the existing urban drainage system, particularly its ability to withstand increasingly intense rainfall events under changing climatic conditions. The flooding of several key areas brought economic and social activities to a standstill, underscoring the need to strengthen Colombo’s urban flood resilience through improved drainage infrastructure and effective stormwater management.

According to reports, approximately 129 mm of rainfall were recorded within a few hours. Officials revealed that the existing drainage system had originally been designed to accommodate approximately 30 mm of rainfall per hour. Meanwhile, some argue that Colombo’s drainage capacity has been significantly enhanced through several infrastructure development projects implemented in recent years and attribute the recent flooding primarily to blockages in the drainage network.

However, attributing urban flooding entirely to heavy rainfall would be an oversimplification. While extreme weather can trigger flooding, the severity and duration of its impacts are often determined by inadequate infrastructure, poor maintenance, unplanned urban development and weaknesses in urban water management.

Beyond heavy rainfall: Understanding the real causes

One of the most likely causes of drainage failure in a city is the accumulation of solid waste and debris in drainage channels. Plastic bottles, polythene, discarded food containers and household waste frequently obstruct roadside drains, culverts and canals. Absence of a proper garbage collection system can even be another contributing factor. Silt deposition at the bottom of drains due to soil washed away from urban construction sites is another issue. Even a properly designed drainage network can become ineffective when it is blocked by waste materials. Recent discussions following the Colombo floods also identified improperly disposed waste as a contributing factor to blocked drains and canals. Regular maintenance, responsible waste disposal and stronger enforcement of environmental regulations are therefore essential.

The second major concern is insufficient drainage capacity. Urban drainage systems must be designed according to rainfall intensity, catchment characteristics, land-use patterns and expected future development. When rainfall exceeds the system’s design capacity, water cannot be discharged quickly enough, resulting in surface flooding. Hence, it is important to reassess the historical design criteria in light of climate-induced changes in rainfall patterns and changes in land use.

Urban development at the cost of nature

Rapid and poorly planned urbanisation is another significant contributor to urban flooding. Colombo city and its surrounding areas have undergone considerable transformation through residential development, commercial buildings, road construction and infrastructure expansion. Unfortunately, this development has often come at the expense of natural drainage systems, wetlands, marshlands and open spaces.

Natural landscapes absorb and temporarily store rainwater, allowing it to infiltrate into the ground or gradually flow into waterways. However, when these areas are replaced by concrete buildings, asphalt roads and paved surfaces, the proportion of rainwater entering drainage channels increases considerably. This increased surface runoff places additional pressure on existing drainage infrastructure.

Studies indicate that the total wetland extent in the Colombo Region declined by approximately 40% between 1992 and 2021, primarily due to urbanisation and land-use changes. The reduction of these green spaces and natural water-retention areas is an important factor contributing to increased flood vulnerability.

Poor connectivity and coordination: A network-wide problem

An effective drainage system is an interconnected network comprising roadside drains, culverts, canals, retention areas, pumping stations, gates and final discharge points such as rivers or the sea. If one section of this network is blocked, damaged or undersized, the performance of the entire system can be affected.

In Colombo, the drainage network involves multiple institutions, including the Colombo Municipal Council, the Sri Lanka Land Development Corporation, the Urban Development Authority and other relevant agencies. Their responsibilities extend across different components of the urban water-management system. Hence, the drainage system should be maintained in a well-coordinated manner to ensure that it functions efficiently. Establishing a single authority to handle the entire drainage system is another option. Integrated drainage planning must therefore consider the entire catchment, from the point where rainwater falls to the location where it is safely discharged.

Building a climate-resilient city

Building a climate-resilient city requires a shift from reactive disaster management to proactive risk reduction. Clearing blocked drains after a flood is necessary, but preventing future floods requires an integrated approach including planning and building climate-resilient infrastructure and the protection of natural ecosystems. 

Individuals and business entities can also contribute to urban flood mitigation by adopting measures such as rooftop rainwater harvesting, green roofs and rain gardens to temporarily retain stormwater. These interventions reduce surface runoff, ease pressure on urban drainage networks and help minimise peak flows during intense rainfall events.

A modern city should not be measured solely by its skyscrapers, highways and commercial developments, but also by its ability to withstand natural hazards while protecting the commercial activities, lives and livelihoods of its people.

(The writer is a water resources engineer)

title: Budgeting for a better Sri Lanka | Daily FT
summary:
Wednesday, 11 November 2026 00:20
-     - 52

The Government serves as the primary governing institution responsible for providing public goods, enforcing law and order, ensuring economic stability, and advancing national development goals. To carry out these wide-ranging economic and social functions, the sovereign state must systematically raise revenue through taxation, duties, and non-tax channels, and strategically deploy these financial resources across public institutions. The execution of these fiscal responsibilities is governed through public finance frameworks, which dictate how public money is collected, prioritised, managed, and audited.


At the center of public finance lies the legislative instrument known as the Appropriation Bill. Under constitutional standards, such as Article 148 of Sri Lanka’s Constitution, Parliament retains ultimate authority over all public funds, stipulating that no tax may be levied and no revenue withdrawn from the Consolidated Fund without explicit legislative approval.

The Appropriation Bill represents the formal legislative proposal that authorises the Government to withdraw funds from the Consolidated Fund to meet service expenditures, administrative overheads, and development projects for a specific financial year.

Government Budget

The national Budget is the central policy document through which a Government translates its economic strategy, policy promises, and development objectives into binding financial commitments. Beyond being a mere accounting ledger of projected receipts and outlays, the Budget functions as an instrument for macroeconomic stabilisation, resource reallocation, and wealth redistribution. It directly impacts inflation targets, employment figures, national debt levels, private sector investment incentives, and overall economic growth trajectories.

A sound Government Budget typically exhibits several key characteristics that reflect strong public financial management. First, comprehensiveness requires that the Budget capture all Government revenues, expenditures, off-Budget funds, and contingent liabilities to ensure complete financial transparency. Second, fiscal transparency and clarity ensure Budget documents clearly delineate between recurrent operational expenses, such as wages and interest payments, and productive capital investments. Third, predictability and multi-year alignment align annual operational spending allocations with medium-term expenditure frameworks and long-term economic strategy. Fourth, allocative and operational efficiency directs resources toward high-multiplier sectors—such as education, digital infrastructure, and renewable energy—while keeping administrative wastage minimal. Finally, fiscal sustainability demands that expenditure commitments be balanced against realistic revenue projections to prevent unmanageable debt accumulation.

Deficit Government Budgets

A deficit Government Budget occurs when total state expenditure exceeds total Government revenues during a fiscal period, requiring the state to bridge the gap through domestic or foreign borrowing. Most modern developing nations, including Sri Lanka, operate under persistent Budget deficits to finance national development obligations and bridge infrastructure shortfalls.

Budget deficits offer clear advantages when managed strategically. In accordance with Keynesian economic policy, targeted deficit spending stimulates aggregate demand by increasing national employment, boosting consumer purchasing power, and encouraging overall economic activity during downturns. Deficits are particularly beneficial for funding productive capital expenditure, allowing Governments to execute large-scale, high-multiplier capital projects—such as ports, energy grids, and digital networks—that generate long-term economic returns far exceeding their initial borrowing cost. Moreover, deficit financing supports crisis response and social protection, enabling states to maintain social safety nets, healthcare systems, and economic relief programs during crises without making sudden, damaging cuts to public services.

Conversely, persistent Budget deficits introduce significant structural disadvantages. Uncontrolled spending leads to mounting public debt accumulation, forcing future generations to bear heavy debt-servicing burdens that consume large portions of the annual Budget. Deficit spending financed through excessive central bank liquidity expansion or heavy domestic borrowing generates severe inflationary risks, eroding real household purchasing power. Large Government borrowing requirements also cause a crowding-out effect in financial markets by absorbing domestic banking liquidity, pushing up market interest rates and restricting credit access for private sector enterprises. Finally, relying on foreign debt to cover fiscal shortfalls heightens external vulnerability, exposing the nation to foreign exchange volatility, sovereign rating downgrades, and debt sustainability crises.

As Sri Lanka navigates its post-recovery macroeconomic stabilisation trajectory, fiscal policy remains the ultimate litmus test of state priorities. The presentation of the 2027 Appropriation Bill—outlining an estimated state expenditure framework of Rs. 4,992.8 billion—offers a critical empirical window into how the nation balances short-term institutional stabilisation with medium-term growth objectives. While the headline figure of nearly Rs. 5 trillion underscores an expanding state financial footprint, a granular analysis of spending allocations reveals a classic structural duality. On one side stands the ongoing effort to maintain core administrative and social obligations, while on the other lie strategic capital investments aimed at expanding national productive capacity.

A central theme in modern Sri Lankan public finance is the trade-off between recurrent consumption and capital formation. Out of the total Rs. 4,992.8 billion outlay for 2027, Recurrent Expenditure absorbs Rs. 3,240.2 billion, representing 64.9% of total spending. This substantial commitment covers state sector wage bills, operational administrative overheads, debt service interest obligations, and social safety net transfers. In contrast, Capital Expenditure commands Rs. 1,752.5 billion, or 35.1% of the national Budget envelope. While a 35.1% capital expenditure allocation represents a significant improvement compared to the severely constrained capital Budgets during peak crisis years, the structural distribution across line ministries highlights where fiscal rigidity remains firmly entrenched versus where dynamic development is actively prioritised.

The allocation of state funds across functional line ministries exhibits extreme concentration, following an aggressive Pareto distribution pattern. The top five portfolios absorb 65% of the entire Budget envelope, while the top nine portfolios control 90%, accounting for Rs. 4,492.0 billion of total expenditure. Consequently, the remaining 18 ministries and agencies are left to share the residual 10%, totaling Rs. 500.8 billion. This heavy fiscal concentration means that critical future-facing sectors—such as the Digital Economy, Energy, Science and Technology, and Trade—operate within a tight nominal fiscal envelope, necessitating exceptionally high capital efficiency and aggressive private-sector synergies to achieve meaningful economic impact.

Dual-track Budgetary strategy

The 2027 spending framework reveals a distinct dual-track Budgetary strategy operating within the Government apparatus. Traditional administrative domains remain deeply constrained by severe fiscal rigidities, with recurrent allocations consuming the vast majority of available resources in Public Administration at 93%, Public Security at 91%, Provincial Councils at 87%, and Defence at 85%. Heavy state wage bills and baseline operational maintenance costs effectively crowd out discretionary capital initiatives in these sectors, signaling that long-term fiscal relief will depend heavily on comprehensive digital transformation and systematic civil service streamlining.

At the same time, the state’s capital expenditure strategy focuses sharply on high-multiplier productive assets to catalyse economic growth. The Ministry of Housing, Construction and Water Supply leads this shift, with 97% of its total allocation directed toward capital projects, representing Rs. 80 billion out of an Rs. 82 billion Budget. The Ministry of Energy follows closely with 96% allocated to capital investments, totaling Rs. 29 billion out of Rs. 30 billion. Transport, Highways and Urban Development accounts for the single largest physical development commitment at Rs. 432 billion, representing 86% of its Budget, complemented by Rs. 20 billion for the Digital Economy, which constitutes 77% of its overall allocation. By prioritising physical connectivity, energy grid reliability, and modern digital infrastructure over administrative consumption, the state aims to lay the operational foundation necessary for long-term macroeconomic expansion, with the top six ministries capturing approximately 74% of the total national Budget.

Structural vulnerabilities

Despite these targeted investments, significant economic disadvantages and structural vulnerabilities persist across the fiscal landscape. Nationwide, nearly two-thirds of all spending is tied up in recurrent obligations, heavily driven by public sector payroll, operational overheads, debt service, and transfers. Line ministries like Public Administration and Provincial Councils leave virtually no room for discretionary fiscal maneuvering. This high structural weight creates deep Budget rigidities that crowd out vital public investments during economic downturns, limiting the state’s ability to execute counter-cyclical economic interventions when they are needed most.

Human capital development also faces structural headwinds within the current Budgetary architecture. While Education, Higher Education, and Vocational Education combined account for 7% of total spending, the capital component within this envelope remains constrained at just 24% capital versus 76% recurrent expenditure. Underinvesting in modernising primary and secondary classrooms, expanding advanced digital research laboratories, and upgrading vocational training infrastructure threatens to stunt innovation-led growth over the coming decade. Furthermore, the combined operational weight of Public Administration and Provincial Councils consumes over 26% of the entire national Budget—swallowed almost entirely by recurrent operational costs—reflecting an oversized public administration burden relative to Sri Lanka’s current wealth generation capacity.

When benchmarked against developed economies, Sri Lanka’s public finance structure underscores stark comparative differences. Advanced economies typically allocate a much higher percentage of GDP or public Budgets toward long-term future readiness, such as the green energy transition, advanced digital infrastructure, scientific research and development, and comprehensive social safety nets with high automatic stabilisers. While their baseline operational expenditures remain large in absolute terms, a significantly larger fraction of their discretionary spending directly targets productivity-enhancing capital and modern technologies. Sri Lanka, by contrast, remains structurally constrained by a heavy recurrent consumption burden of state wages, debt servicing, and administrative upkeep, leaving a leaner 35% headline capital ratio—much of which remains reliant on external financing or deficit expansion.

A similar divergence appears in public sector scale and operational efficiency. Developed economies place heavy emphasis on digital governance frameworks, automated e-citizen service portals, and lean bureaucratic structures to keep administrative recurrent spending low, thereby freeing up substantial fiscal space for targeted welfare programs and high-multiplier public investments. Sri Lanka continues to face high structural wage bills within its central public administration and provincial setups, directly reducing the net fiscal dividend available for broader economic transformation.

In terms of research, development, and technology integration, advanced industrial nations direct substantial public capital into future-technology domains including artificial intelligence, renewable energy grids, and semiconductor research. In contrast, Sri Lanka’s line items for future-facing domains—such as the Digital Economy at Rs. 26 billion, representing less than 1% of overall spending—receive modest absolute shares. This allocation ratio indicates a persistent lag in fiscal prioritisation for the Fourth Industrial Revolution, leaving the nation vulnerable to global shifts in technology and trade competitiveness.

Decisive policy adjustments

To navigate these structural challenges, decisive policy adjustments must be implemented across three key pillars. First, the state must systematically rationalise public administration by implementing deep structural reforms to curb ballooning recurrent wage and operational bills, explicitly redirecting generated savings toward high-multiplier capital projects. Second, policymakers must enhance capital efficiency by ensuring that major investments in transport, energy, and urban development undergo rigorous cost-benefit analyses, prioritising export-enabling infrastructure that yields measurable macroeconomic returns. Finally, the Government must scale up fiscal allocations for the digital economy, science, and technology to transition Sri Lanka from a factor-driven economy to a resilient, knowledge-driven economy that aligns more closely with developed nation paradigms.

RAWALPINDI: Despite another day lost to bad light and nearly 45 overs lost in total, Pakistan thoroughly dominated the first two days of the first cricket Test against Sri Lanka at the Rawalpindi Cricket Stadium here yesterday.

Sri Lanka finished the second day on 114-3 in reply to Pakistan’s first innings of 434-9 declared to trail by 320 runs and require a further 121 runs to avoid a follow-on. Kamindu Mendis was unbeaten on 40 and with him was former captain Dhananjaya de Silva on 22. On these two rests Sri Lanka’s chances of edging closer to Pakistan’s total.   

Pakistan started the day well from 281-5 with Saud Shakeel and Ghazi Ghori carrying their sixth wicket partnership to worth 96. Shakeel looked all set for a well-deserved ton before unfortunately strangling one down the leg side to provide Asitha Fernando with his 100th Test wicket.

Sri Lanka toiled hard on this pitch which had a bit in it for the pacers, but there were runs on offer as well and Shakeel ensured that he cashed in. Ghori gave him good support but missed out on a maiden Test half-century when he was dismissed for 48 (72 balls, 2 fours). Arafat Minhas was troubled by the short stuff, but he batted positively to make an impressive contribution on debut, throwing his bat around to bring up a fifty – 52 off 72 balls (9 fours, 1 six). Razaullah chipped in with a couple of big hits before both fell in quick succession prompting Babar Azam to declare nine down and have a crack at Sri Lanka for an hour before tea.

The Pakistani pacers made immediate inroads, snatching two early wickets, including the prized scalp of Dinesh Chandimal for one and Pasindu Sooriyabandara without scoring. The skills of Mohammad Abbas and Saqib Khan coupled with disciplined line and length bowling brought the green wicket alive all of a sudden. It seemed to have enough spice for the pacers to continue to extract movement out of it, which was something the Sri Lankan bowlers struggled with, largely due to their wayward bowling.

Lahiru Udara and Kamindu Mendis survived a few nervy moments, including a review and a run-out opportunity before tea. Udara lived dangerously to score 42 off 52 balls (7 fours) before edging a straight forward catch to the wicket-keeper to give debutant Saqib Khan his second wicket after the break. Kamindu Mendis and Dhananjaya de Silva saw Sri Lanka through without any further lapses.

Asitha Fernando broke the 28-year-old record of Chaminda Vaas by becoming the fastest Sri Lankan fast bowler to take 100 wickets achieving it in 48 innings.

Fernando reached that landmark when he had Saud Shakeel caught behind by Kusal Mendis for 93 on the second day of the first Test at Rawalpindi yesterday. The legendary Vaas took three innings more than Fernando to reach that mark in 1998.

In addition to the record, Fernando also has the best bowling average amongst the six fast bowlers from Sri Lanka who have crossed the 100-wicket mark in Test cricket. He averages 27.01 from 29 matches compared to 29.58 from 111 Tests (355 wickets) by Vaas.

Overall, Fernando is the 10th bowler from Sri Lanka to surpass 100 Test wickets. The list includes four spinners – Muttiah Muralitharan 800 wickets, Rangana Herath 433, Dilruwan Perera 161 and Prabath Jayasuriya 134. (ST)

Sri Lanka faces a daunting challenge when they take on hosts Bangladesh in a crucial Group-stage encounter of the 15th SAFF Championship at the National Stadium in Dhaka tonight at 8:00 p.m., with a place in the semi-finals at stake.

Following their disappointing 2-2 draw against Bhutan last Sunday, the Lankans are under enormous pressure to deliver. Having looked set for victory, Sri Lanka let the opportunity slip through their fingers following costly goalkeeping errors by veteran custodian Sujan Perera, who was unable to prevent two goals that could arguably have been saved. However, Coach Abdulla Al Mutairi remains confident despite the setback.

 The equation is now clear for the Lankan camp, with qualification hanging in the balance. A victory or a draw will guarantee them a place in the semi-finals. Even a narrow defeat could keep their hopes alive, depending on the final goal difference and disciplinary record.

The Sri Lankan camp is optimistic about its chances, with the team expected to be at full strength with the return of four players who were on the bench against Bhutan.

“The last game is behind us. We were not at our best, and several factors denied us what could have been a deserved victory. Tonight is virtually a final for us, and the boys are determined to deliver for the country,” said Al Mutairi.

“We know Bangladesh have a well-balanced side with several players capable of changing the game. We have done our homework and will give everything to secure our semi-final berth,” he added.

Much will also depend on experienced goalkeeper Sujan Perera, who will need to put his previous mistakes behind him and produce a composed performance in this all-important encounter.

Meanwhile, Bangladesh are expected to enjoy considerable home advantage, with their overseas-based players adding further strength to an already competitive outfit. Much of the attention will be on Hamza Choudhury and Farhan Ali Wahid, whose experience in English football is expected to boost the hosts’ attacking options.

With passionate home support behind them, Bangladesh will be eager to make their presence felt. The conditions at the National Stadium could also play a significant role, with the prevailing weather likely to influence the pace of the game.

For Bangladesh, the encounter also serves as an important test ahead of Saturday’s semi-finals, where they could potentially meet either India or Pakistan.

Historical statistics favour the hosts. Since their first meeting in 1979, the two nations have faced each other on 18 occasions, with Bangladesh recording 11 victories, Sri Lanka winning five and two matches ending in draws.

With history favouring Bangladesh and the home crowd firmly behind them, Sri Lanka will have to rise to the occasion. For the Lankans, tonight is more than just another match — it is a battle for survival and a golden opportunity to march into the last four of the tournament.

Achraf Hakimi will hope to defend his title of African Footballer of the Year on December 2 as he leads a trio of Moroccan players on the shortlist, which does not feature Egyptian star and former winner Mohamed Salah.

Morocco Captain Hakimi is joined by Brahim Diaz and Ismael Saibari on the 10-man shortlist released by the Confederation of African Football (CAF) last week.

The trio led Morocco to a controversial Africa Cup of Nations (AFCON) title in January. Although Senegal beat Morocco 1-0 after extra time in the final, Morocco were subsequently awarded the title after Senegal walked off the pitch over a disputed penalty. A decision on Senegal’s appeal over being stripped of the title will be made at the end of November.

The three players also helped Morocco reach the quarterfinals of the World Cup, where Saibari was the country’s top scorer with three goals while Hakimi scored one.

Salah’s absence from the list has raised eyebrows because the Egyptian forward is widely recognised as a generational talent and one of Africa’s top players. The former Liverpool star, now with the Turkish side Trabzonspor, took home the award in 2017 and 2018. Mane won the subsequent two awards.
